## WF2 RESILIENT DELIVERY v1.0

**Setup: one credential.**

1. `Append Dead Letter (Google Sheets)` -> select your Google Service Account credential.
2. In the same spreadsheet as Workflow 1, add a second tab named `Dead_Letter`
   with these headers in row 1:

`correlation_id | timestamp | contractor_id | reason | attempts | last_error | last_http_status | payload_json | alerted`

The sheet ID is already set as a literal on that node. Both stub endpoints are public
echo services, so nothing else needs configuring.

**How to demonstrate each requirement**

Success             -> post a valid payload. Expect 200 `delivered`, 1 attempt.
Retry then recover  -> point `emailUrl` at a flaky endpoint.
Retries exhausted   -> add `"_demo_force_failure": true` to the payload. The sender is
                       switched to an unreachable port, so all 4 attempts fail fast.
                       Watch the loop run in the execution log, then the dead-letter row
                       appear, then the alert fire. Expect 502 `retries_exhausted`.
Permanent failure   -> point `emailUrl` at a 4xx endpoint. ONE attempt, no retries,
                       straight to dead letter.
Malformed payload   -> see the note in SCOPE AND HONESTY.

**Publish the workflow and use the production URL.**

## Design decisions

**The retry is a loop on this canvas, not a node setting.** `Send Email` has n8n's own
`retryOnFail` switched OFF deliberately. `Evaluate Attempt` classifies the response,
`Retries Remaining?` decides, `Wait Before Retry` backs off, and the wire runs back into
the HTTP node. Every attempt is therefore visible in the execution log and every
decision is inspectable, which a hidden node-level retry never is.

**Only retryable failures are retried.** Transport errors, 5xx and 429 retry.
Any other 4xx is a permanent client error and goes straight to the dead letter, because
retrying a rejected recipient four times only delays the alert by seven seconds.

**Exponential backoff with jitter.** 1s, 2s, 4s, capped at 8s, plus up to 25% random
jitter. Without jitter, every execution stalled by a provider outage retries in lockstep
the moment it recovers and knocks it over again.

**Dead letter is written BEFORE the alert.** If the alert channel is also down, the
record still exists. Persistence first, notification second.

**Alerting is an allowlist.** Only `retries_exhausted` and `permanent_failure` page
anyone, because only those mean <COMPANY>'s pipeline failed. A malformed body, an invalid
payload and a failed validation are all recorded in the dead letter and none of them
wake anyone at 3am. Alert fatigue is how real alerts get ignored.

**The `alerted` column records intent, not state.** It says whether this record
warranted a page, which is true at write time and stays true. Marking it "sent"
afterwards would need a second update-by-key write against the same row; that is
deliberately out of scope here, and the alert's actual outcome is in the HTTP response
and the execution log.

**A validation failure is recorded but does not page anyone.** It is the caller's to fix
and cannot be replayed. An exhausted delivery is <COMPANY>'s problem and does page. Both are
persisted, because "nothing is silently lost" is not the same as "wake someone up".

## Scope and honesty

**Where malformed JSON is actually caught.** If a caller declares
`Content-Type: application/json` and sends invalid JSON, n8n's HTTP layer rejects it
before any node runs and returns its own structured JSON error. No node can catch that.
Nothing crashes and nothing is half-processed. If the body arrives as text, Raw Body
hands it to `Validate and Normalise`, which catches the parse failure and returns this
workflow's own 400 `invalid_json`. Both are graceful; they are owned by different
components. To see the second path, send the malformed body as `text/plain`.

**2xx means accepted by the provider, not delivered to the human.** The response says
`delivered` in the sense the provider accepted it, and the attempt history is returned
so the caller can see exactly what happened.

**If the dead-letter write itself fails**, the response says so explicitly rather than
returning a clean error. An audit gap you cannot see is worse than one you can.

**Reusability.** The block from `Build Failure Record` to `Send Alert` is the pattern
Workflow 4 reuses. In a longer engagement it would be extracted into a shared sub-workflow
called via Execute Workflow, so onboarding, payment chasing and screening all fail the
same way. It is kept inline here so each submitted workflow imports and runs alone.
